strengths: Elegant stepwise decomposition approach that principally addresses the challenge of trajectory optimization in discrete diffusion models by decomposing into tractable per-step posteriors
Strong theoretical framework with Theorem 4.1 establishing equivalence between stepwise and trajectory optimization, plus convergence guarantees (Prop 4.3)
Generality of framework handling arbitrary reward functions, subsuming prior methods like DPO as special cases

Comprehensive multi-domain experimental validation (DNA design: 12.3% improvement; protein folding: superior ddG; language modeling: consistent gains) with multiple metrics demonstrating reward optimization without over-fitting
Practical advantages over RL-based baselines (DRAKES) including no need for online sampling per iteration and superior sample efficiency
Thorough ablation studies on key hyperparameters (β, N, iterative labeling) with interpretable results
weaknesses: Additive factorization assumption in Theorem 4.1 is restrictive and lacks empirical validation—no analysis of trajectory-level rewards in practice or performance degradation when assumption is violated

Scope considerably narrower than claimed: all theory and experiments limited to masked diffusion with MASK tokens; applicability to other discrete diffusion variants (categorical noising, absorbing states) is stated but undemonstrated

No computational efficiency analysis despite claims of 'efficient optimization'—missing wall-clock time comparisons with DRAKES and complexity analysis of forward process q(x_t|x_0) sampling at each step

Hyperparameter design lacks principled justification: w(t)=1-α_t motivated via theory but then given ad-hoc token-amortization reinterpretation; β varies drastically across stages (0.92→0.064) without clear selection criteria

Modest language modeling improvements (78.6→80.7 on GSM8K is 2.1% absolute gain) only on 8B model with no comparison to other LLM preference optimization methods or concurrent diffusion alignment work
Stepwise reward definition r̂_t uses learned posterior p_θ, introducing distribution mismatch bias not analyzed; self-normalized importance sampling variance-bias tradeoff in Eq. 12 also unanalyzed
Reward model reliability inadequately addressed—only brief discussion of noisy/harmful rewards without empirical analysis of robustness or degradation curves
Iterative labeling variant introduced without clear distinction from offline algorithm; insufficient comparison of offline vs. iterative performance
Limited baseline comparisons: most from [59] using reported numbers; no direct comparison with concurrent diffusion alignment methods (DPO-Diffusion, DSPO) on identical tasks

strengths: Addresses relevant problem of preference optimization for discrete diffusion models, which is understudied compared to autoregressive models
Technically sound mathematical framework with correct derivations and proofs for main theorems
Demonstrates consistent empirical improvements across three diverse application domains (DNA design, protein folding, language modeling)
Loss formulation generalizes beyond DPO's Bradley-Terry restriction to work with arbitrary reward functions
Clever use of importance sampling with p_ref as proposal enables efficient offline optimization
Comprehensive ablation studies on hyperparameters (β, N, iterative labeling) with detailed hyperparameter specifications in appendix
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited: stepwise decomposition is straightforward decomposition of trajectory objectives; distribution matching loss is standard importance sampling-based cross-entropy between Boltzmann policies already known from inverse RL
Theorem 4.1 assumes restrictive additive reward factorization without discussion of when this holds in practice or how it fails for trajectory-level evaluations

Significant theory-practice gap: theory requires exact stepwise rewards but practice uses finite-sample Monte Carlo approximation; Proposition 4.3 only guarantees asymptotic equivalence with no finite-sample error bounds
Incomplete experimental validation: primary baseline is only DRAKES; missing comparisons to cited diffusion alignment methods [58, 63, 22, 69] that should be included
Language modeling improvements are modest and lack statistical significance testing: GSM8K +2.1%, IFEval +2.2%, no error bars; claims to surpass LLaMA-3-8B unsubstantiated
Extreme hyperparameter sensitivity and variance: β ranges 0.92→0.064, N ranges 25→918 across stages; unclear if hyperparameters were validated on held-out sets (overfitting risk)
Contradicts 'offline optimization' positioning by introducing iterative labeling (Sec 5.4) requiring 10k-12.8k additional reward labels, making method semi-online
Weak intuition provided for why stepwise posterior alignment improves trajectory alignment beyond computational tractability; no guidance on when to apply method or which reward properties favor SDPO
Missing ablations: w(t) choice not studied despite being introduced without justification; sample size N shows inconsistent patterns across domains without principled guidance
Protein inverse folding results show success rate decrease (78.6%→75.5%) despite improved Pred-ddG, indicating unexamined reward-quality tradeoffs

strengths: Novel stepwise decomposition framework elegantly decomposes intractable trajectory-level optimization into tractable per-step posterior alignment, well-suited to discrete diffusion models
Sound theoretical contributions with Theorem 4.1 establishing equivalence between stepwise and trajectory objectives, and Propositions 4.2-4.3 guaranteeing correctness of the empirical loss

Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse domains (DNA, protein, language) with consistent improvements: 12.3% over DRAKES on DNA design, GSM8K 78.6→80.7, 30.9% relative improvement on AlpacaEval
Methodological generality: works with arbitrary reward functions (overcomes DPO's Bradley-Terry restriction) and reduces to DPO as special case
Thorough ablation studies examining β sensitivity, sample size N effects, and iterative labeling, with clear interpretable results
Clear presentation, strong baselines (CG, SMC, TDS, CFG, DRAKES), and detailed hyperparameters supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Theorem 4.1's additive factorization assumption r̂(x₀:T,c) = Σₜ w(t)r̂ₜ(xₜ,c) is restrictive with no analysis of performance under violation; lacks empirical validation that used reward models satisfy this property

Core empirical loss (Eq. 12-13) is a standard Monte Carlo approximation of KL divergence between Boltzmann policies; fundamental novelty is primarily in applying existing preference optimization machinery to stepwise decomposition
Language modeling improvements are modest (2.1 points on GSM8K) without error bars or statistical significance tests; only 2 epochs of UltraFeedback training suggests potential undertaining

Incomplete experimental comparisons: no direct comparison with other discrete diffusion alignment methods [58,69]; language model evaluated only against base model, not other preference optimization methods on same architecture

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity with dramatically different β values across tasks (0.92, 0.4, 0.064 for DNA; 0.047, 0.063 for protein) requiring task-specific tuning; limited guidance for practitioners

Missing implementation details: computational cost vs baselines not discussed (especially for iterative labeling); justification for always using pre-trained model as reference; reliance on iterative labeling for DNA/protein contradicts 'offline' framing
Minimal failure analysis: only brief limitation discussion; no empirical study of behavior with noisy/misspecified reward functions despite mentioning this limitation

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: preference optimization for discrete diffusion models with fundamentally different structure from autoregressive models
Novel stepwise decomposition approach that elegantly decomposes trajectory alignment into per-step posterior alignment, enabling efficient computation and compatibility with arbitrary rewards
Theorem 4.1 provides theoretical connection between stepwise objectives and trajectory alignment under additive reward factorization
Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse domains (DNA design, protein folding, language modeling) with consistent improvements: 12% over DRAKES on DNA activity, GSM8K 78.6→81.2
Principled optimization framework based on KL-divergence distribution matching that generalizes beyond Bradley-Terry model assumptions to arbitrary reward functions
Thorough ablation studies examining effects of β, sample size N, and iterative labeling strategy
Practical offline method scaling to 8B language models without requiring online sampling during training
Multiple evaluation metrics across tasks demonstrate robustness against reward hacking
Strong empirical results with standard deviations reported across 3 random seeds
weaknesses: Theorem 4.1 exhibits circular reasoning: the chain reward r̂(x₀:T) is derived from the stepwise problem definitions, making the equivalence proof somewhat circular rather than providing independent motivation for the stepwise approach

Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.1 assumes exact solutions to subproblems but practical algorithm uses self-normalized importance sampling with finite samples and biased partition function estimates; no convergence analysis or approximation error bounds provided

Design choices lack principled justification: w(t)=1-αₜ scheduler only justified informally as per-token amortization; sample size N has limited guidance with Table 4 showing plateau; β values differ dramatically across tasks (0.92, 0.047, 1.0) without principled selection strategy

Complex experimental setup obscures contribution isolation: DNA results require 3-stage training with different hyperparameters and iterative relabeling adding 10k labeled samples over 2 rounds; Figure 3 shows iterative labeling provides substantial gains but its contribution to total improvement unclear

Limited baseline coverage in some domains: language modeling only compares D2-DPO, not VRPO which is compared for DNA/protein; DRAKES uses different algorithmic approach (RL with Gumbel-softmax) making fair comparison challenging
Restricted additive factorization assumption: Theorem 4.1 requires reward to decompose additively over diffusion steps; limited analysis of when this holds, fails, or impacts performance degradation

Reproducibility concerns: multi-stage training is complex with task-specific design choices (e.g., protein uses finetuned checkpoint as reference in Stage 2 but DNA uses original); no code release mentioned; sensitive to pre-trained models from [60]

Missing computational cost analysis: Appendix B.4 provides theoretical complexity but no wall-clock time comparisons with baselines for varying N; practical overhead of Monte-Carlo sampling not characterized

Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed: Tables 8-9 show significant performance variations with β but provide minimal guidance on selection; different β values across tasks suggest limited transferability
Language modeling improvements modest in relative terms (2.6 point absolute gain on GSM8K) compared to DNA/protein results

strengths: Well-motivated stepwise decomposition approach that tractably handles trajectory alignment for discrete diffusion models
Theoretical contribution (Theorem 4.1) establishing equivalence between stepwise and trajectory optimization objectives
General framework handling arbitrary reward functions, beyond prior methods limited to Bradley-Terry assumptions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse domains (DNA design, protein folding, language modeling) with consistent improvements
Thorough ablation studies on key hyperparameters (β, N, dataset size, iterative labeling)
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theorem 4.1's additive reward factorization assumption is unstated and unclear when it holds for practical rewards; users specify r(x₀,c) but the induced trajectory reward may not decompose additively
Monte Carlo approximation in Eq. 10 introduces unquantified bias for partition functions, yet theoretical guarantees (Theorem 4.1) assume exact optimization; convergence analysis missing
Key design choice w(t)=1-αₜ in Eq. 12 lacks principled justification, introduced only to 'amortize loss to tokens' with post-hoc interpretations and no ablations
Complex multi-stage experimental setup with varying hyperparameters across stages (β: 0.92→0.4→0.064) and reference model switching obscures algorithmic contributions and reproducibility
Incomplete baseline comparisons: recent competitors (D2-DPO, VRPO from 2025) barely explained; algorithmic differences vs. D2-DPO unclear; missing equal-compute comparisons with online RL methods
Iterative labeling variant critical to results (Fig. 3) but disconnected from main theory (Sections 4.1-4.3) and lacking specification; deviates from claimed offline setting
No robustness analysis against reward model noise/errors despite acknowledging in Appendix D that such models may be unreliable in practice
Missing convergence guarantees, sample efficiency analysis, and characterization of when the method fails or underperforms; no guidance on choosing SDPO vs. alternatives

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing a genuine challenge in preference optimization for discrete diffusion models with well-motivated stepwise decomposition approach
Strong theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.1 elegantly establishes equivalence between stepwise posterior optimization and trajectory-level objectives through additive reward factorization
General framework compatible with arbitrary reward functions, generalizing beyond Bradley-Terry model assumptions (unlike DPO/D2-DPO)
Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse domains (DNA, protein, language) with consistent improvements: 12.3% on DNA, strong gains on protein, GSM8K 78.6→81.2
Well-ablated experimental design: multiple metrics per task (reward + naturalness), strong recent baselines, proper ablations on β, N, and iterative labeling
Practical and interpretable design choices: w(t)=1-α_t for amortizing loss per token, connection to DPO via Bradley-Terry simplification
Clear presentation with informative visualizations (Figure 1), comprehensive appendices with detailed proofs and hyperparameters
weaknesses: Theoretical assumption of additive reward factorization (Theorem 4.1) not thoroughly explored: unclear when arbitrary rewards satisfy this property and consequences of violations
Biased Monte Carlo estimation in Eq. 10 acknowledged but not formally analyzed; no convergence guarantees or analysis of how finite-N bias affects optimality
Significant hyperparameter tuning required: β varies substantially across stages (0.92→0.064 for DNA), and ablations show non-monotonic sensitivity, limiting principled application
Incomplete baseline comparisons: D2-DPO/VRPO comparisons use prior work results not direct reimplementation; language modeling lacks DRAKES comparison and autoregressive baselines

Reproducibility gaps: forward process sampling implementation unclear, number of diffusion steps per iteration unspecified, UltraFeedback version and preference pair construction for LM task not detailed
Limited failure analysis: brief limitation section only mentions noisy rewards; no discussion of when iterative labeling is necessary, reward model sensitivity, or failure modes
Modest language modeling improvements (GSM8K +2.6 points) and comparison to different base model (LLaMA-3-8B vs LLaDA-8B) weaken claims generality
